Greetings FatPeopleHelp, I know it's been a while since anyone posted here, but I just wanted to share with you my experiences with exercise and weight loss a couple years ago. Apologies for the clickbait-esque title.

I used to be a fatass. Not hamplanet-sized, but visibly overweight (BMI ~25). My parents were constantly nagging me about losing weight, and my mom even yelled at me whenever I ate too much or gained weight. I was tired and sleepy for most of the day, and when I was forced to run a mile at school, I had to walk for a significant portion and ended up horrendously out of breath at the end. Running was my worst nightmare and needless to say, something had to be done.

So, one summer, following my parents' suggestion, I started jogging 3 miles nonstop every morning.

The first day, it was absolute hell. As expected, even though I was listening to fast heavy metal on my headphones, I was panting heavily by the end of the first mile. I had to jog very slowly, almost in place, for a while. By the time the second mile came around, I was almost limping. But I gritted my teeth, shouted a few times while exhaling (fortunately no one else was in close proximity to hear me), and carried on. After the third mile was complete, I lurched forward, almost hyperventilating, and refused to run any further.

The second day, much to my surprise, was noticeably better. While I was still completely out of breath after the first mile, I didn't remember it feeling like hell. In fact, I was able to complete the first mile and a half without mentally complaining about how tough it was, etc. However, because of the first day, my legs were trembling and felt like jello afterwards. It hurt, but it was somehow a good feeling. A feeling that I've achieved something.

Progressively, the jogging sessions became easier, and it took fewer times to get rid of the fear than I thought. After a week, I was out of bed by 8 AM clamoring to have my 3-mile morning run. I also ditched my headphones so that I could regulate my pace better.

Even after just a week, my legs were getting noticeably slimmer, and the fat in my arms and legs were slowly becoming less dense. I was instantly able to focus better on my work, had more energy during the day, and fell asleep faster at night. After about two months, at a karaoke party, I even found that I was able to sing better and with a fuller, more sustained sound.

It used to take me 40 minutes to complete my run, and now it takes 30 minutes. I've lost 20 lbs, gotten a lot stronger since then and am much more able to deal with academic stress than before. Of course, that effect was achieved by coupling running with regular stretching and simply eating half the amount I used to eat.

The moral of the story is, running does wonders to your body and mind.
